clue.text: Troop meantime demolished Eastern power

indicators.note: something demolished is knocked down and its materials can be rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, thirteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Soldiers wreck something in the interval while an oriental state looks on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Troop' looks like a verb or a body of soldiers, but it is simply letters to be reshuffled with 'meantime'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ottoman Empire was the Turkish state that ruled much of the Middle East and Balkans for six centuries.

clue.text: Old pop song often called for in cafés?

blocks.note: first meaning: a 1920s standard from the musical No, No, Nanette
second meaning: a couple ordering a pot of the hot drink between them

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second half is a literal reading of the song title: an order a pair of customers might place.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is both a famous jazz-age standard and the everyday request a couple makes when ordering drinks.

clue.text: Supervise parts of Test by middle of week

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central portion, so only the inner letters are kept

blocks.note: a cricket Test match is divided into overs of six balls each
the two central letters of the four-letter word

explanation.surface: Someone is told to invigilate sections of an exam held midweek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Test' reads like an exam, but capitalised it is a Test match in cricket, whose units of six deliveries are overs.
explanation.definitionFit: To supervise work is to watch over it and direct it, which is exactly what oversee means.

clue.text: Irregular feature showing my mastery, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals one of several possible versions, so the letters may be put in another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boastful craftsman points to a quirky detail as proof of skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Showing' joins the definition to the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of balance between two sides is an irregularity, a feature where things fail to match.

clue.text: Limb, after decapitation, remains?

indicators.note: decapitation removes the head, so the leading letter goes

blocks.note: an arm or leg is a member of the body

explanation.surface: A grisly scene: a severed arm is what is left after a beheading.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a corpse, but 'remains' with its question mark means what is left of a fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A glowing fragment left in a dying fire is one of the last remnants of what burned.

clue.text: Passengers accepting adjustment of toll – it’s the same for everyone

indicators.note: an adjustment alters how something is set, so these letters are rearranged
to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: PAX is the travel-industry abbreviation for passengers
taken as written

explanation.surface: Travellers put up with a revised road charge that everyone must pay alike.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a descriptive phrase: a poll tax charges every adult the same flat amount. It was notoriously introduced in Britain in 1990.
explanation.definitionFit: A head tax levies an identical fixed sum on each person regardless of income, hence uniform for all.

clue.text: Lexicographer mostly heard and understood tense

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the final letter is cut

blocks.note: radio operators say roger for message received
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A dictionary-maker listened carefully and grasped the nervous mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like an adjective for anxious, but it is the grammar term abbreviated. Roger is radio-speak for message received.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Mark Roget compiled the famous Thesaurus, a word reference organised by meaning.

clue.text: Curative plant has a life in South Carolina, America

indicators.note: one thing in another sits within it, so a piece is placed inside

blocks.note: SC is the postal abbreviation for South Carolina
taken as written
a bio is a short life story
US is the abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: A medicinal herb is thriving in the American South.
explanation.walkthrough: The two state and country abbreviations sit either side of the pieces that go in.
explanation.definitionFit: Scabious is a wildflower once used to treat scabies and other skin complaints, hence a healing plant.

clue.text: Long party held after college

indicators.note: an event held after another comes later, so this piece follows the other

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for college
a rave is a large dance party

explanation.surface: A lengthy celebration takes place once term at college is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' sits at the front looking like an adjective describing the party, but it is the verb meaning yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: To long for something is to yearn or hanker after it, the same desire as to crave.

clue.text: Nothing in Times, reflected hoodlum

indicators.note: something in another is enclosed by it, so one piece sits inside
a reflection in a mirror shows things the wrong way round

blocks.note: as in multiplication: three times four is three by four
the figure zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A thug featured in The Times newspaper is nothing much.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make 'Times' the newspaper, but it means the multiplication sign read aloud as a word. A yob is British slang for a lout, itself the word backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A yob is a rowdy young lout, the British equivalent of a street thug or ruffian.

clue.text: Run off, right?

blocks.note: first meaning, as two words: to flee, British slang for running away fast
second meaning: legitimate, genuine and above board

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense splits the answer into two words, to leg it, British slang for to scarper. The question mark warns of the informal second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To leg it is slang for fleeing on foot, and the single word is slang for lawful or genuine.

clue.text: Coastal measure, new, abandoned by country after it flipped over

indicators.note: something flipped over is turned the other way round
what is abandoned is left behind, so that letter drops out of the word
coming after means placed later, so this piece follows the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the Scandinavian nation
N is the abbreviation for new; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: A shoreline gauge is left behind by a nation after it capsizes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' gives N, the letter the country abandons. 'Country' looks like the subject, but it is the word that loses a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tidemark is the line left on a beach showing how far up the shore the water reached.

clue.text: Crowd, taken aback about defeat, show signs of progress

indicators.note: taken aback suggests being pushed backwards, so the letters run the other way
about means around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: a mob is a crowd
a defeat is a loss

explanation.surface: Supporters stunned by a defeat still detect improvement in the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken aback' reads as surprised, but it sends the crowd backwards before it wraps the defeat.
explanation.definitionFit: To blossom is to develop and flourish, as a flower opens, so it means improving visibly.

clue.text: Went round area? Declined to cover that

indicators.note: to cover something is to go over and around it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: to decline in condition is to decay or rot
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: Someone did the rounds of a district but refused to take it on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Declined' looks like refused, but it means decayed; 'that' points back to the area as the thing covered.
explanation.definitionFit: To rotate is to turn about an axis or take turns in sequence, both senses of going round.

clue.text: Bishop will appear in a trial if all goes well

indicators.note: appearing in something means showing up inside it, so one piece goes within

blocks.note: taken as written
a trial is a test
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A cleric is due to give evidence at a court hearing, assuming nothing goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trial' suggests a courtroom, but here it is just a test.
explanation.definitionFit: At best introduces the most optimistic outcome, what happens when everything turns out favourably.

clue.text: Extravagant lecturer, getting university cross, beginning to avoid panel

definitions.note: adjective here; the answer is a noun used attributively, as in luxury goods

indicators.note: to avoid the beginning is to skip it, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for lecturer
U is the abbreviation for university
an X is a cross
a jury is a panel of judges

explanation.surface: A spendthrift academic annoys the university and dodges a disciplinary committee at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as angry, but it is the letter shaped like a cross.
explanation.definitionFit: Used before a noun, luxury describes lavish, costly things such as hotels or cars, so it works as an adjective.

clue.text: Where one’s placed to start meal, having secured a place to live?

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece holds another inside

blocks.note: lunch is a midday meal
taken as written
a pad is slang for a flat or home

explanation.surface: A newcomer asks where to sit for the first meal now they have found somewhere to live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To start meal' looks like a starter course, but 'Where one's placed to start' is the definition; the meal is lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: A launch pad is the platform rockets lift off from, figuratively any springboard for a new venture.

clue.text: Official, reprimanded after old city wiped out, thought again

indicators.note: what is wiped out is erased, so those letters vanish from the word

blocks.note: a ref (referee) is a match official
to lecture someone is to scold them
Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A referee who was told off once an ancient city was destroyed reconsidered.
explanation.walkthrough: Ur, the ancient Mesopotamian city, is the crossword's favourite old city; it vanishes from the middle of the scolding.
explanation.definitionFit: To reflect is to think carefully or ponder, especially on past events, so it means reconsidered.

clue.text: No, though I might risk mine?

definitions.text: No, though I might risk mine?

blocks.note: surface reading: an emphatic refusal
setter's reading: I might gamble my own existence, but I won't bet yours

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is an idiomatic emphatic no; the clue takes it literally, as a speaker willing to stake their own existence but not someone else's.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a forceful refusal, meaning absolutely not under any circumstances whatsoever.

clue.text: Work, having no money, time after time denied protective gear

indicators.note: something denied is withheld or refused, so the named letters are taken away

blocks.note: toil is hard work
skint is British slang for broke
T is the abbreviation for time, once per piece; both are removed

explanation.surface: A broke labourer, again and again refused, goes without safety equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time after time' means T after T: each piece loses its T (time). Skint is British slang for having no money.
explanation.definitionFit: An oilskin is a waterproof coat of oiled cloth, worn by sailors and fishermen against the weather.

clue.text: Part of vessel drags, leading to trouble

indicators.note: what leads to something comes before it, so this piece goes first

blocks.note: to lug is to drag something heavy
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: A section of a ship is towed and causes difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble' looks like a noun, but it is the verb, as in what ails you.
explanation.definitionFit: A lugsail is a four-cornered sail hung from a yard, one component of a boat's rigging.

clue.text: See 8
Waste material, deteriorating almost entirely

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the final letter is cut

blocks.note: food going bad is going off
all means entirely, wholly

explanation.surface: Rubbish rotting away almost completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' is the British sense of food that has gone bad. 'Waste material' is fair because offal originally meant the parts that fall off in butchering.
explanation.definitionFit: Offal is the entrails and organs of a butchered animal, historically regarded as refuse or scraps.

clue.text: Fine pace shown in film

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
a lick is a fast speed, as in going at a fair lick

explanation.surface: A movie presents a pleasing tempo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lick' for pace comes from the British phrase at a fair lick, meaning quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Flick is informal for a movie, from the flickering of early projected pictures.

clue.text: Flash cut off, but revealing sudden movement

indicators.note: something cut off is shortened, so the final letter is removed

blocks.note: in a flash and in a tick both mean in an instant

explanation.surface: A camera flash fails, yet still catches someone jerking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' suggests light, but it is the moment, as in in a tick, British for in a second.
explanation.definitionFit: A tic is an involuntary twitch of a muscle, typically in the face.

clue.text: Fish associated with a barrel, as it were

definitions.text: associated with a barrel, as it were

blocks.note: first meaning: the tuna, under its older British name

blocks.clueFragment: associated with a barrel, as it were
blocks.note: second meaning: a made-up adjective from tun, a large cask, formed like sunny from sun

explanation.walkthrough: 'As it were' admits the second sense is invented: a tun is a big wine cask, and adding a suffix gives a jokey adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunny is the traditional British name for the tuna, a large ocean fish caught for food.

clue.text: Flash publication held back including article from Paris

indicators.note: held back suggests pulled backwards, so the letters run the other way
to include something is to take it inside, so one piece goes within

blocks.note: a mag is a magazine
le is a French definite article

explanation.surface: Breaking news held over is to include a story from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' reads like a news flash, but it is a brief light; 'article' is the grammatical kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A gleam is a brief bright shine of light, the same as a flash or glint.

clue.text: See 12
Treatment for wound unable to progress beyond emergency room after student’s brought in

indicators.note: what is brought in is taken inside, so a piece sits within another
this sets the order of events: the pieces are joined first, then the insertion happens

blocks.note: stuck fast, unable to move on
past means beyond, as in past the house
L for learner, as on British learner-driver plates
ER is the abbreviation for emergency room

explanation.surface: A patient's injury can't be dealt with past casualty once a trainee doctor is involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Student' is L because learner drivers in Britain display an L plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A sticking plaster is the British term for an adhesive bandage put over a small cut.

clue.text: Family name, during second year, carrying little weight

indicators.note: what happens during something falls within it, so the pieces sit inside

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
kin are relatives
N is the abbreviation for name
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A family's surname was barely noticed in a sophomore year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Family name' looks like a surname, but the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Skinny describes a very thin person, someone who bears hardly any body fat.

clue.text: Daughter beginning to reject Prince? Fool

indicators.note: what is rejected is thrown out, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
a prelude is an opening piece
Pr is a standard abbreviation for prince; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A girl starts to turn down a royal suitor, and is called a fool for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince' looks like the suitor, but it is the abbreviation Pr that drops out of the opening.
explanation.definitionFit: To delude is to deceive or mislead someone, making a fool of them.
